 Days After Clocks Fell Back, Study Finds Permanent Daylight Saving Time Would Add 2 Billion Dark School Commutes
 By 
 Lucas Caldwell 
 Published: Nov 09 2026, 4:47 AM EST 
 Facebook 
 Twitter 
 Linkedin 
 Comment 
 Mail 
 Yauhen | Adobe Stock 
 Most of the country set its clocks back an hour on Sunday, Nov. 1, bringing earlier sunrises just as families settle into winter school routines . A new University of Washington study shows what would happen if that switch stopped for good: millions of children would start walking, biking, and waiting for buses before the sun comes up.
 Under permanent daylight saving time, U.S. students would make at least 2 billion more school trips in the dark each year, the researchers estimate in Current Biology . Their more precise extrapolation lands at about 2.14 billion.
 The finding lands while the Sunshine Protection Act, which the U.S. House passed in July, waits in the Senate. If it becomes law, the clock change families just went through would be the last one.
 The Commute Numbers, State by State
 The team combined enrollment figures, each school's listed start time and its exact location to calculate how often students would travel before sunrise. They started with 14 of the 19 states that have already approved permanent daylight saving time if Congress allows it: Washington, Oregon, Idaho, Utah, Colorado, Wyoming, Oklahoma, Louisiana, Tennessee, Mississippi, Alabama, Georgia, Maine and Delaware.
 Across those 14 states, the change would add about 356 million dark-morning commutes a year, with every state seeing an increase, according to a University of Washington release . Georgia would see the largest jump, about 71 million extra trips. Washington would add nearly 35 million.
 Mississippi and Alabama show how local school schedules magnify the effect. Schools there start on average before 8 a.m., and each state would climb from roughly 2 million dark trips today to more than 20 million.
 Communities on the western edge of their time zones would be hit hardest, because the sun already rises later there by the clock.
 The sunrise math explains why. Under permanent daylight saving time, AccuWeather calculated that on Jan. 15, 2027, the sun would rise at 8:10 a.m. in Boston and 8:35 a.m. in Kansas City — well after many school buses have already made their rounds.
 Why the Count Is Likely Too Low
 The national estimate assumes students leave home around 8 a.m. Many leave much earlier, especially those riding buses in rural districts or arriving for breakfast programs and early activities.
 "That's pretty late, so our calculation is likely an underestimation of the real number," lead author Guadalupe Rodríguez Ferrante, a UW postdoctoral scholar in biology, said in remarks reported by ScienceDaily .
 The researchers also used the start time listed for each school, not the earlier time many students must actually be on campus. In rural areas with long bus routes, children can be picked up well before 7 a.m.
 The study also counted only school trips. Parents commuting to work, high schoolers driving themselves, and children walking to bus stops before dawn all fall outside the total.
 The Biology of Morning Light and Teen Sleep
 The concern goes beyond visibility. Bright morning light is the strongest signal that keeps the body's internal clock synchronized with the day, and that clock helps regulate sleep, mood, and appetite.
 Children on fixed school schedules may miss that natural light entirely in winter if they spend early mornings in the dark and the rest of the day indoors.
 Teenagers face a particular problem. During adolescence, the biological clock shifts later, which is why many districts have pushed high school start times back. The researchers argue permanent daylight saving time would effectively undo much of that progress by moving the clock an hour away from solar time all winter.
 Senior author Horacio de la Iglesia, a UW biology professor, has studied this question for years. His earlier work in Seattle found students slept more after high schools moved start times later. On the new findings, he put it plainly: "Nobody wants their kids to go to school in the dark." 
 Some lawmakers have suggested starting school later to compensate. De la Iglesia argues that would simply push work and evening schedules later too, which amounts to realigning daily life with standard time anyway.
 Crash Risk and What the Data Do Not Show
 The team also analyzed U.S. traffic collision records. Fatal crashes involving school-aged pedestrians were roughly twice as likely during dark mornings as after sunrise.
 That finding comes with an important limit. As FOX 6 noted , it does not establish how many additional crashes permanent daylight saving time would cause. Driver behavior, traffic volume, crossing guards, and lighting all vary, and the study did not model those factors.
 Supporters of permanent daylight saving time point to brighter evenings, more after-school daylight and fewer disruptive clock changes. The new study does not weigh those benefits. It measures one specific cost, the number of school commutes that would shift into darkness.
 What Families Can Do Now
 Nothing changes this winter — the Senate has not acted, and federal law still requires the twice-yearly switch, so standard time remains in place until March.
 Families with children who leave before sunrise can still reduce risk. Reflective strips on backpacks and jackets, small clip-on lights and bright clothing make young pedestrians easier to see. Parents can review routes that avoid busy roads without sidewalks and remind teens that phones and earbuds reduce awareness at crosswalks.
 For sleep, getting outdoor light soon after waking, even on a short walk, helps anchor the body clock, while dimming screens in the evening helps teens fall asleep earlier. Parents can also follow the Sunshine Protection Act's progress and share views with their senators, since the bill's fate will decide whether next fall's clock change happens at all.

 What did the study find? Permanent daylight saving time would add at least 2 billion school commutes in the dark each year in the U.S., with a more precise estimate of about 2.14 billion.
 Which states would be most affected? Among the 14 states studied, Georgia would see the largest increase, about 71 million extra dark trips. Mississippi and Alabama would each rise from about 2 million to more than 20 million.
 Why do researchers think the estimate is too low? It assumes students leave home around 8 a.m., but many leave earlier for buses, breakfast programs, or activities.
 Are dark mornings more dangerous for kids? Fatal crashes involving school-aged pedestrians were about twice as likely on dark mornings as after sunrise, though the study did not estimate how many extra crashes the change would cause.
 Is permanent daylight saving time law now? No. The House passed the Sunshine Protection Act in July, but it has stalled in the Senate.
 How can families stay safe on dark mornings? Use reflective gear and lights, choose safer routes, and encourage outdoor light exposure after waking.
